en: The Sūtra on the Analysis of Giving, Spoken by the Buddha.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heavens, Imperially Appointed Grand Officer of the Court of State Ceremonial,
Acting Minister of the Court of Reception, and Great Master of the Transmission of the Dharma, Subject Shi Hu, in accordance with the Imperial Edict.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Kapilavastu, the residence of the Śākyas, in the Nyagrodha Grove, together with a community of bhikṣus.
At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī named Mahāprajāpatī who came to the place where the Buddha was, carrying a new cotton garment.
Having arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This new cotton cloth was made by my own hands; I offer it to the World-Honored One. I only pray that you will accept it, so that I may obtain great benefit and happiness for a long night.”
At that time, the Buddha said to Mahāprajāpatī:
"You may take this cotton cloth and offer it to the great assembly; the merit you shall obtain will be no different from that of making offerings to us."
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī addressed the Buddha again, saying:

“I originally conceived this intention solely for the sake of the World-Honored One to create these robes; I pray that the Buddha will accept them, so that I may obtain great benefit and happiness throughout the long night.”
Thus he entreated him three times with earnest persistence, and the Buddha likewise replied three times:
"One should simply practice impartial giving to the great assembly; the merit obtained will be no different from mine."
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, attending at the side of the Buddha, having witnessed this event, came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This Bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī is the Buddha’s own kin; she possesses great kindness and virtue, which only the Buddha himself knows.”
May the Buddha accept this offered robe; now is the very time to do so, so that Mahāprajāpatī may obtain great benefit and happiness throughout the long night.
The Buddha said, “Ānanda! So it is, so it is!”
"This Mahāprajāpatī is my own kinswoman and possesses great kindness and virtue; this I myself well know.
That she has now come in person to offer me robes she has fashioned with her own hands is truly a most difficult thing to do."
Why is this? Ānanda,
you should know that it is an exceedingly rare thing for any person (pudgala) to be able to give rise to pure faith and take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.

Furthermore, such a person is even more difficult to find who can uphold the precepts of a lay follower (*upāsaka*), namely: abstaining from killing, abstaining from stealing, abstaining from sexual misconduct, abstaining from false speech, and abstaining from intoxicants.

How much more so for the Buddha, the World-Honored One! Having joined their palms in reverent prostration and practiced giving, they possess pure faith and are free from doubt regarding the Buddha; likewise, they have no uncertainty concerning the Dharma and the Saṅgha, and have forever severed all doubts and wrong views regarding the principles of the Four Noble Truths—suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

Ānanda! This bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī has now been able to give rise to pure faith and take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; she has received and upholds the precepts of a lay follower—namely, not killing, not stealing, not engaging in sexual misconduct, not lying, and not drinking intoxicants—and she has already severed all doubt regarding the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, as well as the principles of the Four Noble Truths: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. That this bhikṣuṇī was able to accomplish what is difficult to accomplish is something the Buddha himself knows.
“Ānanda! There are fourteen ways of measuring generosity.
What are these fourteen?
First, practicing giving toward those suffering from illness;
second, practicing giving toward those who have broken the precepts;
third, practicing giving toward those who uphold the precepts.
Fourth, one practices giving to those who have become free from passion;
fifth, one practices giving to those practicing for the fruit of stream-entry;
sixth, one practices giving to those who have attained the fruit of stream-entry.
Seventh, practicing giving while on the path toward the fruit of once-returner;
eighth, practicing giving while abiding in the fruit of once-returner;
ninth, practicing giving while on the path toward the fruit of non-returner.
Tenth, practicing giving toward those on the path to the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala);
eleventh, practicing giving toward those on the path to arhatship;
twelfth, practicing giving toward those who have attained the fruit of arhatship.
Thirteenth, they practice giving toward the pratyekabuddhas;
fourteenth, they practice giving toward the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
Ānanda! You should now know this:
one who gives to a person suffering from illness obtains double the merit.
Giving to one who has broken the precepts yields a hundredfold merit;
giving to one who maintains the precepts yields a thousandfold merit;
giving to one who is free from defilement yields a hundred-thousandfold merit.
Giving to one who is a candidate for the fruit of stream-entry yields immeasurable merit; how much more so, then, to one who has attained the fruit of stream-entry!
Giving to one who is a candidate for the fruit of once-returning yields immeasurable merit; how much more so, then, to one who has attained the fruit of once-returning!
Giving to one who is a candidate for the fruit of non-returning yields immeasurable merit; how much more so, then, to one who has attained the fruit of non-returning!
Giving to one who is a candidate for arhatship yields immeasurable merit; how much more so, then, does giving to one who has attained the fruit of arhatship?
Giving to all pratyekabuddhas yields immeasurable merit; how much more so, then, does giving to a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha?
This is called the comparative measurement of the merit of fourteen kinds of giving.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!
You should know that there are seven kinds of giving to the great assembly:
first, giving to the assembly of bhikṣus present before the Buddha;..."
Second, making offerings to the community of bhikṣus after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa;
third, making offerings to the community of bhikṣuṇīs after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa;
fourth, making offerings to both the communities of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
Fifth, to give to the community of bhikṣus who travel abroad to teach and transform after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa;
sixth, to give to the community of bhikṣuṇīs who travel abroad to teach and transform after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa;
seventh, to give to both communities of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs who travel abroad to teach and transform after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
These are called the seven kinds of assemblies to whom one should practice giving.
"Furthermore, Ānanda,
you should know that there are four kinds of purity in giving."
What are the four?
First, the purity of the giver is such that there is no recipient;
second, the purity of the gift is such that there is no recipient.
Third, the purity of the recipient means there is no giver;
fourth, the purity of what is received means there is no giver. Ānanda!
What is meant by "the purity of the giver such that there is no recipient"?

It means that because the giver does not grasp at signs, his physical action is pure, his verbal action is pure, his mental action is pure, his right livelihood is pure, and his view is also pure. Being thus complete, there is no sign of giving; because there is no giving, there is no recipient.
If the donor perceives signs of duality, then their three karmas of body, speech, and mind are not pure; their life is not pure, and their pure vision is also not pure.
If they are free from such signs, then both the donor and the recipient are pure.
"Furthermore, what is meant by 'the purity of the gift such that there is no recipient'?

If the recipient’s bodily action (*kāyakarman*) is impure, their verbal action (*vākkarman*) is impure, their mental action (*manaskarman*) is impure, their livelihood (*ājīva*) is impure, and their view (*dṛṣṭi*) is impure, then the characteristic of a gift exists.

If the recipient’s three actions are pure, their livelihood is pure, and their view is pure—being thus fully endowed—they are without the characteristic of a gift; because they are free from characteristics, the gift is pure."
Furthermore, what is meant by "the purity of the recipient being such that there is no giver"?
If the recipient’s three karmas of body, speech, and mind are not pure, if their livelihood is not pure, and if their views are not pure, then there is the characteristic of a recipient;
if one is free from these characteristics, then there is no giver.
Furthermore, what is meant by "the purity of that which is received is such that there is no giver"?
It means that because the three karmas of the giver are pure, their livelihood is pure, and their view is pure, there is nothing given;
because they are free from giving, there is nothing received, and for this reason, that which is received is pure.
"Ānanda! If one can understand in this way, one will attain the fourfold purity of giving.

At that time, after the Bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī had heard the Buddha proclaim these various methods of giving, she took those robes and offered them to the great assembly; thereupon, the community of bhikṣus accepted them.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"In future ages, if there are faithful sons of good family who are able to give rise to pure faith toward the great assembly and practice giving, you should know that such persons will obtain immeasurable merit; how much more so for those who practice giving in the present?"
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the Venerable Ānanda and the Bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī were filled with joy and exultation; they accepted it with faith and practiced accordingly.
The Sūtra on the Analysis of Giving Spoken by the Buddha
